newsitem.title: USA: Goodyear posts loss; sets output pact with Japan's Sumitomo.
newsitem.headline: Goodyear posts loss; sets output pact with Japan's Sumitomo.

text.p: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. said Wednesday it lost more than $408 million in the fourth quarter, mainly due to a huge charge to adjust the book value of a crude oil transmission pipeline.

The company also announced plans to sign an agreement next week with Japan's Sumitomo Rubber Industries that would call for the two companies to manufacture tires for one another in the United States and Japan.
The pact would avoid creating overcapacity in the industry, it said.
The Akron, Ohio-based company also said its board approved a three-year, $600 million stock buyback programme.
Goodyear said it lost $408.2 million, or $2.63 a share in the fourth quarter, compared with profits of $146.4 million or 96 cents a share a year earlier. Sales were flat at $3.27 billion.

Goodyear said it took charges totalling $872.5 million in the fourth quarter, including a $755.6 million charge to write down the book value of its All American Pipeline -- a major crude oil transmission system.
The charges also hurt its 1996 earnings, which fell to $101.7 million, or 66 cents a share, compared with 1995 earnings of $611 million, or $4.02 a share.
It said the strong dollar hurt its oversease revenues, reducing sales to $13.11 billion from $13.17 billion in 1995.

The company said it expects to sign a production agreement next week with Sumitomo Rubber and two of its affiliate -- Dunlop Tire Corp. and OHTSU Tire & Rubber Co Ltd. -- for up to 2 million passenger and light truck tires a year.

Under the pact, which would run through Dec. 31, 2000, Goodyear will make tires for Dunlop and OHTSU Tire & Rubber Co. Ltd. in North America while Sumitomo Rubber will produce tires for Nippon Goodyear in Japan.

"By better utilizing the existing manufacturing assets of both companies, this agreement would avoid creating overcapacity in the industry," said Goodyear Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Samir G. Gibara. "It also would reduce the exposure of both companies to future economic cycles in the United States and Japan."
Goodyear's stock dropped 50 cents to $54.75 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
